sec.title: Question
sec.p: Among patients with gastric cancer and peritoneal metastasis, does adding intraperitoneal paclitaxel to intravenous paclitaxel plus S-1 improve overall survival compared with intravenous paclitaxel plus S-1?

sec.title: Findings
sec.p: In this randomized clinical trial that included 222 patients with gastric cancer with peritoneal metastasis, intraperitoneal and intravenous paclitaxel plus oral S-1 resulted in significantly longer overall survival than intravenous paclitaxel plus S-1 alone (19.4 vs 13.9 months) without increasing grade 3 or 4 adverse events.

sec.title: Meaning
sec.p: The findings of this randomized clinical trial potentially provide an encouraging signal that intraperitoneal paclitaxel may enhance first-line treatment of gastric cancer with peritoneal metastasis.

sec.title: Importance
sec.p: Gastric cancer with peritoneal metastasis has a poor prognosis, and survival with commonly used regimens, such as intravenous paclitaxel plus S-1 (an oral fluoropyrimidine), remains limited. Whether intraperitoneal paclitaxel, which achieves high drug concentrations in the peritoneal cavity, can improve survival has not been established in a phase 3 randomized clinical trial.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: To determine whether adding intraperitoneal paclitaxel to intravenous paclitaxel plus S-1 improves overall survival in gastric cancer with peritoneal metastasis.

sec.title: Design, Setting, and Participants
sec.p: This multicenter, open-label, randomized phase 3 superiority clinical trial (DRAGON-01) was conducted in 9 hospitals in China. Enrollment went from May 2017 to March 2022, and the data cutoff was March 11, 2025. The trial included adults with gastric adenocarcinoma and laparoscopically confirmed peritoneal metastasis without extraperitoneal metastases or prior systemic therapy.

sec.title: Interventions
sec.p: The IP group received paclitaxel, 50 mg/m2, intravenously plus 20 mg/m2, intraperitoneally on days 1 and 8 of each 21-day cycle, with oral S-1, 80 mg/m2, once per day on days 1 to 14. The PS group received paclitaxel, 70 mg/m2, intravenously on days 1 and 8, with S-1 80, mg/m2, once per day on days 1 to 14.

sec.title: Main Outcomes and Measures
sec.p: The primary end point was overall survival. Secondary end points included progression-free survival and safety.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Among 222 treated patients (median [IQR] age, 59 [48-66] years; 104 [46.8%] female individuals and 118 [53.2%] male individuals), median (IQR) follow-up was 72.2 (50.8-80.2) months. Of 246 who were assessed, 238 (96.7%) were randomized 2:1 to receive intraperitoneal and intravenous paclitaxel plus oral S-1 (IP group) or intravenous paclitaxel plus S-1 (PS group); 222 (90.2%) received treatment (primary analysis). Median overall survival was 19.4 months (95% CI, 17.1-22.9) in the IP group and 13.9 months (95% CI, 10.3-16.1) in the PS group (hazard ratio, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.50-0.90; P = .01). Median progression-free survival was 11.2 months (95% CI, 9.3-14.0) vs 7.2 months (95% CI, 5.7-11.6) (hazard ratio, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.54-0.96). Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 57 (38.5%) in the IP group and 31 (41.9%) in the PS group; no treatment-related deaths occurred.

sec.title: Conclusions and Relevance
sec.p: The results of this randomized clinical trial of patients with gastric cancer with peritoneal metastasis suggest that adding intraperitoneal paclitaxel to intravenous paclitaxel plus S-1 significantly improved overall survival without increasing severe toxic effects, potentially providing an encouraging signal for IP therapy in first-line treatment of gastric cancer with peritoneal metastasis.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Gastric cancer is the fifth most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide and remains a leading cause of cancer death.1 Peritoneal metastasis (PM) is a common pattern of spread in advanced disease and is associated with poor prognosis, with a median survival of 5 to 11 months despite contemporary systemic therapy.2,3,4 Major guidelines recommend first-line systemic chemotherapy, with targeted agents or immunotherapy when indicated, yet the peritoneum remains the main site of treatment failure.5,6,7,8 In East Asia, regimens based on tegafur/gimeracil/oteracil (S-1, an oral fluoropyrimidine) are a standard first-line option and are supported by phase 3 randomized clinical trials.9,10

Delivering paclitaxel directly into the peritoneal cavity in combination with systemic therapy has been proposed to overcome limited drug penetration into peritoneal lesions.10,11,12 The pharmacologic profile of paclitaxel, which is slow peritoneal clearance and prolonged local residence, makes it well suited to this route.12,13 Our phase 2 study in Chinese patients supported the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of intraperitoneal (IP) paclitaxel, informing the design of this phase 3 randomized clinical trial.11,14 Phase 2 studies from Asian centers have reported encouraging outcomes, including median overall survival (OS) of 12.8 to 43.2 months and conversion surgery rates of 41.9% to 78.0%; however, most were small, single arm, heterogeneous, and limited by short follow-up.11,15,16,17,18,19,20,21 To our knowledge, the only prior phase 3 randomized clinical trial (PHOENIX-GC) tested the same IP regimen against a different systemic regimen (S-1 plus cisplatin) and reported a nonsignificant OS difference; however, crossover of control arm patients to IP therapy may have attenuated the treatment effect.10 Therefore, a confirmatory trial that isolated the IP contribution and prespecified conversion surgery criteria was needed.

We conducted DRAGON-01, a multicenter, open-label, randomized, phase 3 clinical trial to test the hypothesis that adding IP paclitaxel to intravenous (IV) paclitaxel plus S-1 would improve OS compared with IV paclitaxel plus S-1 alone in patients with gastric cancer and PM.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: DRAGON-01 was a multicenter, randomized, open-label, phase 3, parallel-group superiority trial that was conducted at 9 hospitals in China with facilities for laparoscopy and IP port placement (Supplement 1 and Supplement 2). The trial was reported following the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) reporting guideline. Enrollment occurred from May 10, 2017, to March 9, 2022. Enrollment and follow-up overlapped with the COVID-19 pandemic from early 2020; the trial was never suspended, and no clinically significant treatment delays occurred. The protocol was approved by the Ruijin Hospital ethics committee and the institutional review boards of all participating centers. An independent data and safety monitoring committee oversaw participant safety at prespecified intervals. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Patients and the public were not involved in the study design. No substantive protocol changes were made after trial initiation.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: Eligible patients were aged 18 to 75 years and had histologically confirmed gastric adenocarcinoma and laparoscopically confirmed PM, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status score of 0 to 1, an expected survival of at least 3 months, and adequate organ function. The upper age limit of 75 years was intended to select patients who were likely to tolerate the protocol therapy and surgery.22 Key exclusion criteria included extraperitoneal distant metastases (ovarian involvement alone was permitted), prior anticancer therapy, and gastric outlet or bowel obstruction; the full criteria are provided in eTable 1 in Supplement 3. All enrolled patients were ERBB2-negative (immunohistochemistry, 0/≥1 or ≥2, with negative fluorescence in situ hybridization results); microsatellite instability and programmed cell death ligand 1 status were not routinely assessed and are unavailable.

sec.title: Randomization and Masking
sec.p: After laparoscopic confirmation of PM, patients were randomly assigned (2:1, favoring the IP group for safety data accumulation and recruitment)10,23 to the IP group (IP and IV paclitaxel plus S-1) or PS group (IV paclitaxel plus S-1). Randomization was centralized via a secure web-based system using a computer-generated sequence. No stratification factors were prespecified because the eligibility criteria defined a clinically homogeneous population. Allocation was concealed until assignment; investigators entered eligibility data, and the system issued assignment. Site staff had no access to future allocations. The trial was open-label; masking was not feasible owing to the nature of the interventions.

sec.title: Interventions
sec.p: In the IP group, an IP port was placed by experienced surgeons using standardized techniques across centers. Patients received IV paclitaxel, 50 mg/m2 and 20 mg/m2, intraperitoneally on days 1 and 8 of each 21-day cycle, plus oral S-1, 80 mg/m2, once per day on days 1 to 14. The PS group received IV paclitaxel, 70 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8, plus S-1 80 mg/m2, once per day on days 1 to 14. On each administration day, the paclitaxel dose (70 mg/m2) was matched between groups, with 20 mg/m2 redirected intraperitoneally in the IP group. Dose interruptions and reductions were applied per protocol (eMethods in Supplement 3). In both groups, treatment continued until disease progression, unacceptable toxic effects, or patient withdrawal. Crossover between treatment groups was not permitted.

Conversion surgery was considered after local multidisciplinary review when prespecified protocol criteria were met, including negative peritoneal cytology results and confirmation by computed tomography (CT) and diagnostic laparoscopy (Supplement 1). Gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy was recommended with R0 intent. Postoperatively, protocol chemotherapy was resumed; in patients without recurrence, S-1 and/or IP paclitaxel could continue to be administered until progression or unacceptable toxic effects (eFigure 1 in Supplement 3).

sec.title: Outcomes and Measures
sec.p: The prespecified primary outcome was OS, which was defined as the time from randomization to death of any cause. Participants who were alive at the data cutoff were censored at the last date that is was known they were alive. Secondary end points included progression-free survival (PFS), which was defined as time from randomization to first documented progression or death and assessed by investigators using contrast-enhanced CT at baseline and every 3 cycles. There was no independent central imaging review. Progression of measurable disease was evaluated per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), version 1.1 (European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer). For patients without measurable peritoneal lesions, progression was defined as new lesions or clear nontarget progression on CT. Peritoneal disease extent was graded according to the Japanese Classification (third English edition)24 and Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI).25 Other secondary end points were conversion surgery rate, major pathological response rate in resected primary tumors (Becker grade 0-1),26 and adverse events. Pathological assessment was performed at each center without central review. Safety was evaluated before each treatment day; adverse events were graded by the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 5.0 (National Cancer Institute).27 Postoperative complications were graded per the Clavien-Dindo classification within 30 days of surgery.28

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: All analyses followed the prespecified statistical analysis plan (Supplement 2). The trial tested the superiority of the IP regimen for OS. The sample size was calculated using the Schoenfeld method, assuming a median OS of 19 vs 11 months, 2:1 randomization, 2-sided α of .05, 90% power, uniform accrual over 6 years, and 3 additional years of follow-up, yielding a required sample of 171; planned enrollment was increased by 30% to 222. Efficacy analyses used the modified intention-to-treat (mITT) population (all randomized participants who received ≥1 dose), which was analyzed as assigned. Post hoc sensitivity analyses were performed in the full intention-to-treat population and with study site as a covariate. OS and PFS were estimated by Kaplan-Meier analyses; 95% CIs used the Brookmeyer-Crowley method, with log-log transformation. Treatment groups were compared with log-rank tests; hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs were obtained from unstratified Cox proportional hazards models. The proportional hazards assumption was evaluated using Schoenfeld residual-based tests. Binary outcomes were compared using χ2 or Fisher exact tests. Adverse events were summarized descriptively. Missing data were not imputed. No interim efficacy analyses were planned; the data and safety monitoring committee could recommend discontinuing for safety concerns only. All tests were 2-sided (P < .05). Analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.2; R Foundation) at the data cutoff of March 11, 2025.

sec.title: Study Population
sec.p: Between May 10, 2017, and March 9, 2022, 246 patients were assessed for eligibility; 238 (96.7%) were randomized to the IP group (158 [66.9%]) or the PS group (80 [33.6%]). Before initiating therapy, 16 withdrew consent (IP, 10 [6.3%]; PS, 6 [7.5%]), yielding an mITT population of 222 (IP, 148 [66.7%]; PS, 74 [33.3%]; Figure 1). All 16 subsequently received IV chemotherapy outside the protocol. Median follow-up, which was estimated by the reverse Kaplan-Meier method, was 72.2 months (IQR, 50.8-80.2). Baseline characteristics were balanced (Table 1). The median (IQR) age was 59 (48-66) years; 104 (46.8%) were female and 118 (53.2%) were male. Baseline peritoneal cytology results were positive for 73 (49.3%) in the IP group and 38 (51.4%) in the PS group. The median PCI score was 15 (IQR, 9.0-23.0) in the IP group and 14 (IQR, 8.0-22.8) in the PS group. Vital status was ascertained for all 222 participants; no patients were lost to follow-up for the primary end point, and there were no missing data for key baseline covariates or the primary outcome.

sec.title: Efficacy Outcomes
sec.p: At data cutoff, 132 (89.2%) in the IP group and 69 (93.2%) in the PS group had died. Median OS was 19.4 months (95% CI, 17.1-22.9) in the IP group vs 13.9 months (95% CI, 10.3-16.1) in the PS group (HR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.50-0.90; P = .01). OS rates at 1, 2, and 3 years were 69.6%, 37.2%, and 25.0% vs 54.1%, 20.3%, and 12.2%, respectively. A post hoc sensitivity analysis in the full intention-to-treat population (n = 238) yielded consistent results (HR, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.51-0.90; P = .01; eFigure 2 in Supplement 3). PFS was also longer with IP (median, 11.2 months [95% CI, 9.3-14.0] vs 7.2 months [95% CI, 5.7-11.6]; HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.54-0.96; P = .02; Figure 2). The proportional hazards assumption was not violated for OS (Schoenfeld test) or PFS. In an exploratory piecewise Cox analysis, the OS treatment effect emerged at 3 to 6 months, strengthened through 9 to 12 months, and peaked at 12 to 18 months (HR, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.21-0.75) before attenuating beyond 24 months (eFigure 3 in Supplement 3). Post hoc subgroup analyses showed no evidence of heterogeneity across prespecified subgroups (Figure 3). Adjustment for study site did not change the treatment effect estimates for OS (HR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.48-0.87; P = .004) or PFS (HR, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.54-0.95; P = .02).

sec.p: The median total treatment cycles were 12 (IQR, 8-20) in the IP group and 8 (IQR, 4-15) in the PS group. Treatment was discontinued mainly because of disease progression, unacceptable toxic effects, or port-related complications. The median (IQR) relative dose intensity was 86.1% (80.6%-92.1%) to 91.1% (84.9%-96.9%) in the IP group and 91.8% (85.1%-97.4%) to 95.8% (90.8%-99.3%) in the PS group. Treatment was de-escalated to maintenance for 95 (64.2%) in the IP group and 18 (24.3%) in the PS group.

In an exploratory analysis, among those with positive peritoneal cytology results at baseline, conversion to negative cytology was more frequent with IP than with PS (61; 83.6% vs 52.6%; P = .001). Second-look laparoscopy was performed for 92 (62.2%) in the IP group and 40 (54.1%) in the PS group. Conversion surgery was undertaken for 75 (50.7%) in the IP group and 26 (35.1%) (P = .04) in the PS group at a median of 5.2 months (IQR, 3.3-6.6) and 4.3 months (IQR, 3.5-5.1) from randomization, respectively. R0 resection was achieved for 63 (84.0%) in the IP group and 22 (84.6%) in the PS group. The major pathological response in resected primary tumors was observed in 14 of 75 (18.7%; 9.5% of the entire IP cohort) in the IP group and 9 of 26 (34.6%; 12.2% of the entire PS cohort) in the PS group. In exploratory analyses, median OS among patients who underwent conversion surgery was 33.1 months (95% CI, 26.6-39.3) in the IP group and 18.8 months (95% CI, 16.0-41.4) in the PS group; among those who did not, median OS was 11.1 months and 10.0 months, respectively (eFigure 4 in Supplement 3).

In patients with progression or recurrence, the peritoneum was the most common first site of failure (95 [64.2%] in the IP group and 57 [77.0%] in the PS group). Other frequent first sites included the ovaries (21 [14.2%] vs 7 [9.5%]), liver (14 [9.5%] vs 5 [6/8%]), and nonregional lymph nodes (7 [4.7%] vs 2 [2.7%]). Among patients with disease progression, second-line therapy was received by 100 (71.9%) in the IP group and 57 (81.4%) in the PS group; in the IP group, 97 (97.0%) continued concurrent IP chemotherapy (eTable 2 in Supplement 3). Anti–programmed cell death 1 antibodies were received by 19 patients (12.8%) in the IP group and 7 (9.5%) in the PS group across subsequent lines. In an exploratory postprogression survival (PPS) analysis, median PPS was 5.7 months in the IP group and 4.5 months in the PS group (HR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.51-0.96; P = .03; eFigure 5 in Supplement 3). Additional exploratory analyses of OS by resection status and landmark postsurgical OS and PFS are presented in eFigures 6 and 7 in Supplement 3.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: No treatment-related deaths occurred (Table 2). Grade 3 to 4 adverse events occurred for 57 (38.5%) of the IP group and 31 (41.9%) of the PS group. Common grade 3 to 4 hematologic events included leukopenia (32 [21.6%] vs 18 [24.3%]), neutropenia (29 [19.6%] vs 17 [23.0%]), anemia (17 [11.5%] vs 11 [14.9%]), and thrombocytopenia (8 [5.4%] vs 6 [8.1%]). Among nonhematologic toxic effects, grade 3 to 4 fatigue occurred for 11 (7.4%) and 7 (9.5%), respectively. Grade 2 alopecia (the maximum Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade for this event) occurred for 8.1% (12 and 6, respectively) in both groups. Port-related complications occurred for 40 (27.0%) in the IP group, with 16 (10.8%) requiring surgical intervention; most occurred early in the trial (eTable 3 in Supplement 3). Postoperative complications (Clavien-Dindo grade≥II) after conversion surgery were similar (IP, 21 [28.0%]; PS, 7 [26.9%]; no postoperative deaths; eTable 4 in Supplement 3). Adverse events were summarized descriptively without formal hypothesis testing.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this randomized phase 3 clinical trial, adding IP paclitaxel to IV paclitaxel plus S-1 significantly improved OS in patients with gastric cancer and PM without increasing severe toxic effects. Secondary and exploratory outcomes also favored the IP group, including longer PFS and a higher rate of conversion surgery, which was consistent with improved local control of peritoneal disease, the most common site of failure in this population.

The observed efficacy aligns with the pharmacology of IP paclitaxel. IP administration uses the peritoneal-plasma barrier to maintain high drug concentrations on peritoneal surfaces while limiting systemic exposure.13,29 Despite a lower IV paclitaxel dose in the IP arm, disease control was similar between groups, supporting a direct IP contribution. We also observed more frequent clearance of positive peritoneal cytology results and higher rates of second-look laparoscopy and conversion surgery in the IP arm, which was consistent with improved peritoneal disease control.

To our knowledge, all prior randomized clinical trials of IP chemotherapy in this setting, including the phase 3 PHOENIX-GC trial, have not demonstrated a statistically significant OS benefit in the primary analysis.10 Several differences may explain the discrepant findings. First, our matched-dose design isolated the contribution of the IP route, whereas PHOENIX-GC compared different systemic backbones. Our trial also prespecified conversion surgery criteria. The PHOENIX-GC per-protocol analysis showed a significant advantage for IP therapy (HR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.43-0.94; P = .02), and sensitivity analyses adjusting for baseline ascites also favored the IP arm (P = .01). Population differences between Chinese and Japanese cohorts cannot be excluded.2,30 Despite these considerations, the magnitude and consistency of the survival benefit, together with the long follow-up, provide what is to our knowledge the first randomized phase 3 evidence supporting an OS benefit with IP chemotherapy in this setting. Independent validation in international trials is warranted.

The control regimen (IV paclitaxel plus S-1) was a guideline-listed, first-line option in China at trial design.31 The control arm’s median survival of 13.9 months was within historical ranges.10 For context, the PM subgroup of the chemotherapy-only arm in RATIONALE-305 had median survival of 11.8 months,32 although that subgroup likely included patients with concurrent nonperitoneal distant metastases, limiting direct comparison with our study’s peritoneal-only population.

Current practice favors chemoimmunotherapy.32,33 IP chemotherapy is not intended to replace immunotherapy; it can be combined to strengthen peritoneal disease control.34 In PM subgroups of recent trials, median survival was 12.3 months (RATIONALE-305) and 14.8 months (CheckMate 649)32,33; however, these subgroups included patients with PM irrespective of other distant metastatic sites, so cross-trial comparisons are indirect. Prospective studies that integrate IP paclitaxel with immune checkpoint inhibitors are needed.

Safety was acceptable and consistent with known profiles of paclitaxel and S-1. We saw no signal of excess grade 3 to 4 hematologic or nonhematologic toxic effects with the IP regimen. Port-related complications were manageable in experienced centers, and most occurred early in the trial, suggesting a learning curve effect. These findings support the feasibility of sustained IP treatment in centers with established IP access and care pathways.

The longer OS among IP group patients who were undergoing conversion surgery (33.1 vs 18.8 months), despite similar R0 resection rates, may partially have resulted from postoperative IP maintenance therapy, which may have provided sustained control of residual microscopic peritoneal disease that was undetectable at surgery, an advantage not afforded by postoperative systemic therapy alone in the PS group. However, surgery-stratified comparisons were exploratory, subject to selection and immortal time biases, and should be considered as hypothesis-generating. Landmark analyses from the date of surgery showed numerically favorable but nonsignificant differences (eFigure 7 in Supplement 3).

sec.title: Strengths and Limitations
sec.p: Strengths of the study included multicenter randomization, a prespecified primary end point of OS, laparoscopic confirmation of PM, a cohort with a median PCI score of 15 (higher than commonly reported), and long follow-up (>72 months), providing mature survival estimates. This study also had several limitations. The open-label design is less likely to bias OS but may have influenced clinical decisions, such as the threshold for second-look laparoscopy. The trial was conducted in Chinese centers only, limiting generalizability to Western populations. Center-level variability in surgical decision-making, PCI scoring, and timing of second-look laparoscopy was not controlled, and region-specific PCI subscores were not recorded, limiting the assessment of the anatomical distribution of peritoneal disease between groups. Baseline microsatellite instability and programmed cell death ligand 1 data were not available, limiting characterization in the current biomarker-directed era. Patient-reported outcomes were not collected. The mITT analysis excluded 16 patients who withdrew before treatment. Continued IP chemotherapy in second-line treatment is a potential OS confounder. PFS was assessed by investigators without central review. Exploratory analyses of conversion surgery are post hoc, susceptible to selection and immortal-time biases, and hypothesis-generating.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this randomized clinical trial, IP paclitaxel plus systemic chemotherapy significantly improved survival, with acceptable toxic effects in patients with gastric cancer with PM. These findings provide an encouraging signal for IP therapy in this setting; however, because the chemotherapy backbone does not reflect current first-line standards, future randomized clinical trials are needed to better define the role of IP therapy in the modern era of gastric cancer treatment that involves immunotherapy and other targeted agents.
